changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
changes.change: For engineering leaders at platforms that pay workers, open with the burden, not the map: 'Payments shouldn't be a team.' Follow with the payoff: stop babysitting payments code and unblock the worker-pay roadmap your engineers keep pushing. Use paying workers locally in new countries as the proof point, not the headline.
changes.why: The buyer called this 'an engineering decision' and described brittle payments code ('a haunted house') blocking faster sitter pay for three quarters, which a global-currency opener does not address.

changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For low-ticket platforms whose problem is paying workers, take the acceptance-rate slide out of the pitch. Use that time on the sandbox and on seller onboarding, identity checks and local-currency payouts.
changes.why: The acceptance-rate slide drew silence, and the buyer dismissed it outright: 'our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates.'

changes.current_line: Onboard, verify and pay out to sellers worldwide, in their local currency.
changes.change: For apps that pay workers, use the buyer's words instead of marketplace terms: 'Onboard and verify your [sitters/workers] and handle sitter pay in their local currency, in every country your app launches.' Swap 'sitter' for the buyer's own word for their workers. Do not claim faster payout timing until product confirms it.
changes.why: The marketplace capabilities landed (E19), but the customer says 'sitter pay' and 'the app' rather than 'payouts' or 'marketplace', and their CFO's only question was when sitters get paid.

changes.change: Add a proof point to the developer track for engineering-led evaluations: 'Have your engineers build a working worker-pay flow in our sandbox before you decide.' Pair it with a sandbox starter for that flow, offered early in the evaluation.
changes.why: The deal turned when a customer engineer built a working sitter payment flow over a weekend on our sandbox, after which Daniel 'stopped saying 'if,'' and that happened by chance rather than as a planned offer.
